analysis.body:
Insurance sits in the broader Finance and Insurance category where 36.8% of firms reported using AI in the latest survey period, up from 35.5% the period before, a modest but steady climb that reflects both genuine adoption and the compliance overhead that slows faster movement. The practical work AI is doing in the sector concentrates in underwriting decisioning, claims triage, and fraud detection, all areas where pattern recognition across large structured datasets maps well onto what current models do reliably. These are also the applications that draw the most regulatory attention, which shapes how carriers approach deployment more than in almost any other sector.

The governance layer here is unusually formal. The NAIC model bulletin on insurers' use of AI, adopted by a growing majority of states, is the operative US supervisory document, and the National Association of Insurance Commissioners sets the model-governance and algorithmic-fairness expectations that carriers answer to specifically for underwriting AI. That means any model influencing pricing, eligibility, or claims outcomes faces a compliance review process before and after launch, not as a best practice but as a regulatory expectation. Carriers that treat AI deployment as a pure technology question without engaging the NAIC framework are taking on meaningful legal and operational risk.

The competitive intelligence layer has also become institutionalized. The Evident AI Index provides outside-in benchmarking of major global insurers on AI talent, innovation, leadership, and transparency, functioning as a sector maturity scoreboard that carriers watch and respond to. AM Best has moved in a parallel direction, incorporating innovation and digital maturity into its assessments, which means technology capability now reaches into credit opinion. The signal from both is that insurers cannot treat AI capability as purely internal; it is becoming visible to rating agencies and counterparties in ways that affect cost of capital and market positioning.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the insurance picture is one of real but heavily supervised opportunity. The use cases are proven and the vendor ecosystem is active, but the NAIC framework means that underwriting and claims models require documented fairness testing and governance structures before they go live, and state-by-state adoption of the model bulletin creates a patchwork that national carriers must navigate jurisdiction by jurisdiction. The path to value exists, but the compliance architecture needs to be built in parallel with the technology, not after it.
